<explanation>
Based on the file tree and README content, the project is a Python-based server designed to manipulate Excel workbooks through a set of specialized tools. Its purpose is to allow creating, reading, and modifying Excel files without needing Microsoft Excel installed. The key functionalities include data manipulation, applying formatting, generating charts and pivot tables, managing worksheets, and ensuring validations. In addition, the server uses the Server-Sent Events (SSE) protocol for communication, and it’s designed to integrate with AI tools like Cursor IDE or even be converted for stdio with tools like Supergateway.

Below is a detailed explanation to help you draw an accurate system design diagram tailored to this project’s architecture.

1. Main Components Identification
   • Server Component: This is the central module (src/excel_mcp/server.py) that handles incoming requests, routing, and the SSE transport mechanism.
   • Excel Manipulation Tools: These include modules like calculations.py, formatting.py, chart.py, pivot.py, sheet.py, workbook.py, etc. They encapsulate the specific functionalities for working with Excel files.
   • Utility & Helper Modules: Additional tools such as cell_utils.py, data.py, validation.py, exceptions.py provide auxiliary functionality like data handling, error management, and common error checks.
   • Configuration and Environment: The use of environment variables (e.g., FASTMCP_PORT, EXCEL_FILES_PATH) along with configuration files such as pyproject.toml and uv.lock indicates a runtime configuration mechanism.
   • CI/CD Configuration: The presence of the .github/workflows directory including publish.yml hints at automated workflows for publishing or CI/CD tasks.

2. Relationships and Interactions
   • The Client (or AI tool) sends a request (e.g., to create or modify a workbook) to the server through a specified endpoint, such as the SSE endpoint.
   • The Server processes the request and dispatches it to the appropriate Excel manipulation module (e.g., formatting, pivot generation, or chart creation).
   • Utility modules play a supporting role by processing data, validating inputs, or handling exceptions in these operations.
   • The server then provides a response back to the client via SSE (or via other configured transports as mentioned for remote hosting).

3. Architectural Patterns and Design Principles
   • Modular Design: The project breaks down Excel processing tasks into individual modules, each handling a separate concern (e.g., calculations, chart, pivot). This is an example of separation of concerns.
   • Client-Server Architecture: A central server accepts incoming API requests, processes them by delegating tasks to internal modules, and communicates using the SSE protocol.
   • Extensibility: The design is set up to interact with external AI tools and other services by simply configuring the environment variables or using a conversion layer (e.g., Supergateway). This makes the server both reusable and flexible.

4. Relevant Technologies and Frameworks
   • Python 3.10+: The project uses modern Python as its base.
   • uv (a command-line tool likely for virtual environments and runtime commands) is used for installation and running.
   • SSE Protocol: Server-Sent Events are used for push-based updates to clients.
   • CI/CD with GitHub Actions: Through the .github/workflows configuration.

5. Guidelines for Tailoring the Diagram
   • For a project like this (focused on backend services with a core library for Excel manipulation), the diagram should clearly separate the server logic from the functional modules.
   • Emphasize the data flow starting from external requests (coming from an API client or directly from an AI tool) to the server, and then branching out to the various Excel functionality modules.
   • Clearly indicate environment configuration (variables, configuration files) as they influence behavior and routing.
   • Be certain to include external integration points (like SSE, Cursor IDE customization, and potential remote hosting options).

6. Elements to Include in the Diagram
   • Use clear labels for each component, e.g., “Excel MCP Server (API Entry Point)”, “Excel Processing Modules” (with sub-labels like “Calculations”, “Formatting”, “Charting”, etc.), “Utility Modules”, and “Configuration/Environment”.
   • Draw directional arrows to represent the flow of data:
       ○ Client/Application Request → Server API Endpoint.
       ○ Server → Dispatch/Invoke specific Excel manipulation modules.
       ○ Modules → Return processed results back to the server → Outgoing SSE to client.
   • Use distinct colors or shapes to differentiate between types of components:
       ○ Server component (e.g., use a rectangle with a bold border).
       ○ Modules (group them in a cloud or cluster).
       ○ External services (use a different shape such as a cylinder for configuration/databases or communication endpoints like SSE).
   • Include annotations for the key technical details such as “SSE Protocol”, “Environment Variables (FASTMCP_PORT, EXCEL_FILES_PATH)”, and references to integration guidelines (e.g., AI tool configurations).

By capturing these elements and interactions in your diagram, you will provide a detailed, accurate, and easy-to-understand representation of the project's architecture. This will ensure that anyone reviewing the design, including other developers or stakeholders, gets a clear view of how the system is structured and how each component contributes to the overall functionality of the Excel MCP Server.
</explanation>
